lessons.title: Recognizing maturity signs for sorghum and millet
lessons.body: Knowing when to harvest is critical. If you harvest too early, grain is moist and shrivels; too late, grain shatters and birds eat it. For sorghum, maturity is 90-120 days after planting, depending on variety. Check the hard dough stage: grain is firm, not doughy, and a thumbnail pressed into it leaves a slight dent. The plant leaves turn yellow and dry, but the grain itself should still be slightly soft. For millet, maturity is 75-90 days. The seed head turns from green to brown or grey. Grain at the bottom of the panicle matures first, so test by pressing a few grainsâthey should be hard and not milky. Another sign: when you shake the panicle, mature grain rattles. In Africa, many farmers use bird activity as a sign: when birds start flocking to the field, it's time to harvest. But don't wait too long. For sorghum, if you wait until the whole plant is brown, the grain may shatter. For millet, if the panicle is fully brown and dry, grain can fall off. A simple test: bite a grain. If it cracks between your teeth and is not soft, it's ready. Also, check moisture: grain should be below 20% moisture for harvest. You can use a moisture meter, but if you don't have one, squeeze a handful of grainâif it sticks together, it's too wet. Harvest when 90% of the grains on the panicle are mature. In dry areas, harvest in the morning when dew is gone to avoid shattering. In wet areas, harvest quickly before rains cause mold.

lessons.title: Harvesting methods: hand cutting, sickles, and panicle collection
lessons.body: Harvesting sorghum and millet can be done by hand, with a sickle, or by collecting panicles. Each method suits different scales and conditions. Hand cutting: for small plots, you can snap the sorghum stalk by hand or twist the panicle. This is slow but avoids tools. For millet, you can pull the panicle by hand. But hand cutting can damage the plant and leave grain in the field. A sickle is better: a curved blade with a wooden handle. Cut the sorghum stalk about 30 cm below the panicle, or cut the whole plant at ground level if you want stover for livestock. For millet, cut the panicle with 10-15 cm of stalk. Work in a team: one person cuts, another gathers. A sharp sickle can harvest 0.5-1 hectare per day per person. Panicle collection: for sorghum, you can break off just the panicle by hand or with a small knife. This is faster for grain-only harvest and leaves stalks for fodder. But be careful not to shake the panicle, or grain will fall. For millet, you can collect panicles by hand or use a small sickle. In West Africa, farmers often use a knife to cut the panicle. After cutting, place panicles in baskets or sacks. Don't pile them too highâbruising causes spoilage. If you cut whole plants, tie them in bundles and stand them in shocks to dry. In East Africa, farmers often harvest sorghum by cutting the whole plant and stacking it. For millet, harvest panicles individually. Always harvest in dry weather. If it rains, wait until plants dry. Wear gloves to avoid cuts. Keep harvested grain off the ground to prevent contamination.

lessons.title: Drying and threshing sorghum and millet efficiently
lessons.body: After harvest, grain must be dried to below 13% moisture for safe storage. If too wet, it molds; if too dry, it cracks. For sorghum and millet, drying is done on a clean tarpaulin, concrete floor, or raised platform. Spread grain in a thin layer (5-10 cm) and turn it every 2 hours. Sun drying takes 2-4 days. At night, cover with a tarpaulin to prevent dew. You can test dryness by biting a grainâit should crack, not squash. Or use a moisture meter. For threshing, sorghum and millet need different methods. Sorghum: you can thresh by beating panicles with sticks on a clean surface, or use a mechanical thresher. For small amounts, rub panicles between your hands or use a wooden paddle. Be gentle to avoid breaking grain. Millet: threshing is easier because grain is small. You can rub panicles between your palms or use a mortar and pestle lightly. Or spread panicles and walk on them with clean shoes. For both, thresh on a tarpaulin to catch grain. After threshing, separate grain from chaff by winnowing. If you have many panicles, use a threshing machineâbut rent one if you can't afford to buy. In Africa, many farmers thresh by beating with sticks. But this can crack grain. A better method: use a wooden threshing board with ridges. Or use a tarpaulin and beat with a stick. After threshing, clean the grain. Don't thresh on bare groundâsoil and stones mix in. Also, thresh when grain is dry; if it's too dry, it breaks; if too wet, it smears. Aim for 12-14% moisture for threshing. Store threshed grain in clean sacks.

lessons.title: Cleaning and winnowing grain for market quality
lessons.body: Clean grain fetches a higher price. Buyers reject grain with stones, chaff, or broken kernels. After threshing, you must clean and winnow. Winnowing uses wind to separate lighter chaff from heavier grain. On a windy day, pour grain slowly from a height (1-1.5 meters) onto a tarpaulin. The wind blows chaff away, and grain falls straight down. If there's no wind, use a fan or a winnowing basket. In Africa, farmers use a flat basket (like a shallow bowl) to toss grain into the air. Practice to get the right angle. For sorghum, winnowing is easier because grain is heavier. For millet, grain is small, so winnow gently. After winnowing, remove stones and dirt by hand or with a sieve. Use a sieve with holes slightly smaller than grainâthis lets dirt fall through but keeps grain. For sorghum, a 4-5 mm sieve works; for millet, 2-3 mm. You can also use a gravity separator if available, but it's expensive. For market quality, grain should be uniform in color and size. Remove broken kernels and foreign matter. If you have a lot of grain, use a cleaning machine. But manual cleaning is fine for small scale. After cleaning, bag grain in clean, dry sacks. Don't use sacks that held fertilizer or chemicals. Label bags with date and variety. For premium price, grade grain: remove discolored grains. In some markets, grain is graded as Grade 1 (clean, uniform) and Grade 2 (some foreign matter). Aim for Grade 1. Also, store cleaned grain in a dry place. If you sell, take a sample to the buyer to check quality. Clean grain can increase price by 10-20%.

lessons.title: Using hermetic storage bags (PICS) to prevent weevils
lessons.body: Weevils and other storage pests can destroy your grain in months. Hermetic storage bags, like PICS (Purdue Improved Crop Storage) bags, kill pests without chemicals. PICS bags have three layers: an outer woven polypropylene bag, and two inner high-density polyethylene liners. When you seal grain inside, insects use up oxygen and produce carbon dioxide, which kills them. To use PICS bags: first, dry grain to below 13% moisture. Then put grain in the inner liner, twist the top and tie it tightly with a string or rubber band. Do the same for the second liner. Finally, put the sealed liners inside the outer woven bag and stitch it closed. Store bags on a pallet, not on the floor. Keep away from walls. For sorghum and millet, PICS bags can store grain for 12-24 months without weevils. A 100 kg PICS bag costs about $2-3, but you can reuse it for 2-3 years. If you don't have PICS, you can use metal silos or plastic drums with tight lids. But PICS are affordable and effective. To check if bags are working, look for inflated linersâinsects produce gas. If liners are flat, there may be a leak. Also, never open bags frequently; each opening lets in oxygen. For seed grain, PICS bags preserve germination. In Africa, PICS bags are sold in many agrodealer shops. If you can't find them, you can make a similar system with two plastic bags inside a woven sack. But ensure the inner bags are airtight. Hermetic storage is a game-changer for smallholders.

lessons.title: Building a simple improved granary for long-term storage
lessons.body: For long-term storage, a granary protects grain from pests, moisture, and theft. A simple improved granary can be built with local materials. The design: a raised platform on stones or concrete blocks, with a mud or brick wall, and a thatched or metal roof. The floor should be 50-100 cm above ground to prevent moisture and rodents. The walls can be made of mud bricks, burnt bricks, or woven sticks plastered with mud. The roof should overhang to keep rain out. Inside, you can divide into compartments for different grains. For sorghum and millet, grain should be stored in bags or bulk. If bulk, line the walls with plastic sheeting to keep moisture out. A good granary holds 1-5 tonnes. To build: dig holes for posts, set wooden posts or stones, build a platform of wood or concrete, then walls. Leave a small door with a lock. Ventilation: small holes covered with mesh allow air but keep insects out. For pest control, you can add ash or neem leaves between layers of grain. But hermetic bags inside the granary are better. Also, raise the granary on stones to prevent termites. In West Africa, farmers use mud granaries with thatched roofs. In East Africa, they use elevated wooden granaries. Make sure the granary is dry and clean before storing. Never store grain directly on the floor. Check monthly for leaks or pests. A well-built granary can store grain for 6-12 months. If you can't build a granary, use airtight drums or PICS bags in a dry room. But a granary gives more space and protection. Community granaries can be shared, but ensure good management.

quiz.q: What is a key sign that sorghum is ready to harvest?
options: B) Grain is soft and milky
C) Grain is hard and leaves turn yellow
quiz.explanation: At maturity, sorghum grain becomes hard and plant leaves turn yellow.

quiz.q: For millet, what indicates maturity?
options: A) Panicle turns brown or grey
B) Grain is milky when pressed
D) Panicle is green and moist
quiz.explanation: Millet panicles turn brown or grey when mature.

quiz.q: What moisture level is ideal for harvesting sorghum and millet?
quiz.explanation: Grain should be below 20% moisture at harvest to avoid spoilage.

quiz.q: Which tool is commonly used for harvesting sorghum and millet?
quiz.explanation: A sickle is the standard tool for cutting grain stalks or panicles.

quiz.q: What is panicle collection?
options: B) Breaking off only the grain head
quiz.explanation: Panicle collection means harvesting only the grain head, leaving stalks.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid piling harvested panicles too high?
options: A) It causes bruising and spoilage
quiz.explanation: High piles cause bruising and heat, leading to spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture level for safe storage of sorghum and millet?
quiz.explanation: Grain must be dried to below 13% moisture for safe storage.

quiz.q: How long does sun drying typically take for sorghum and millet?
quiz.explanation: Sun drying usually takes 2-4 days with regular turning.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for dry grain?
quiz.explanation: Dry grain cracks when bitten, while wet grain squashes.

quiz.q: Which method is gentle for threshing millet?
options: C) Walking on it with boots
quiz.explanation: Rubbing panicles between palms is gentle and effective for millet.

quiz.q: Why should threshing be done on a tarpaulin?
quiz.explanation: A tarpaulin prevents soil and stones from mixing with grain.

quiz.q: What is winnowing?
options: A) Separating grain from chaff using wind
quiz.explanation: Winnowing uses wind to separate lighter chaff from heavier grain.

quiz.q: What is the correct height to pour grain during winnowing?
quiz.explanation: Pouring from 1-1.5 meters allows wind to blow away chaff.

quiz.q: What size sieve is recommended for cleaning sorghum?
quiz.explanation: A 4-5 mm sieve lets dirt through but keeps sorghum grain.

quiz.q: Why should you not use sacks that held fertilizer for storing grain?
quiz.explanation: Chemical residues can contaminate grain and harm health.

quiz.q: How much can clean grain increase market price?
quiz.explanation: Clean, well-graded grain can fetch 10-20% higher prices.

quiz.q: What are the three layers of a PICS bag?
options: A) Outer woven, two inner plastic liners
C) Outer plastic, two woven layers
D) One plastic, two paper layers
quiz.explanation: PICS bags have an outer woven polypropylene bag and two inner high-density polyethylene liners.

quiz.q: How do hermetic storage bags kill pests?
quiz.explanation: Insects die when oxygen is depleted and carbon dioxide builds up.

quiz.q: What is the maximum storage time for grain in PICS bags?
quiz.explanation: PICS bags can store grain for 12-24 months without weevils.

quiz.q: How can you check if a PICS bag is working?
quiz.explanation: Inflated liners indicate gas production by insects, meaning the seal is good.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of an improved granary?
quiz.explanation: A raised floor (50-100 cm) prevents moisture and rodents.

quiz.q: Why should a granary have a roof overhang?
quiz.explanation: An overhanging roof protects grain from rain and moisture.

quiz.q: What can be added between grain layers to repel pests in a granary?
quiz.explanation: Ash and neem leaves are natural pest repellents used in traditional storage.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored grain in a granary?
quiz.explanation: Monthly checks help detect pests, leaks, or moisture problems early.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for threshing?
quiz.explanation: Threshing at 12-14% moisture prevents grain breakage and smearing.

quiz.q: Which grain is easier to winnow?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum grain is heavier, making winnowing easier than for millet.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mature millet grain?
options: B) It is soft and milky
D) It sticks to the panicle
quiz.explanation: Mature millet grain rattles when the panicle is shaken.

quiz.q: Why is it important to harvest in dry weather?
options: A) To prevent mold and spoilage
quiz.explanation: Dry weather prevents mold growth and grain spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the first step before storing grain in PICS bags?
options: A) Dry grain to below 13% moisture
quiz.explanation: Grain must be properly dried to prevent mold inside the sealed bag.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a community granary?
quiz.explanation: Community granaries allow sharing of resources and management, but require good organization.
